findings.title: test_basic's time.sleep(0.1) is patched away, making the test racy
findings.body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), so the later `time.sleep(0.1)` intended to 'give flusher threads time to process after drift change' actually does nothing. The flusher thread only picks up the new `current_drift` value on its next loop iteration; if it hasn't run between setting the drift and `step.join()`, the segment is never flushed and `(msg,) = messages` will fail. The test now depends on thread scheduling luck and will be flaky (or silently not exercising the flush path). Use an unpatched sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep` bound before patching, or a real eventfd/condition) instead.

findings.title: Killed flusher processes are never joined, leaking zombies on repeated restarts
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a hung/crashed process is `kill()`ed and immediately replaced via `_create_process_for_shards`, but `join()` is never called on the old process object (it is simply dropped from `self.processes`). With the spawn start method, killed child processes remain zombies until reaped by the parent. Under a scenario where a process repeatedly hangs (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS=10 times), each restart leaks a zombie process (and its pipe/socket resources for the shared `Value` handles). Call `process.join(timeout)` after kill, or otherwise reap the old process before replacing it.

findings.title: join(timeout) skips terminate() for remaining processes once the deadline passes
findings.body: In `join`, once `remaining_time <= 0` the code `break`s out of the outer loop entirely, so any processes not yet waited on are never sent `terminate()`. They are only released via the `stopped` flag, which the child checks at most once per ~1s iteration (and only after completing any in-flight produce/flush work). If a child is stuck producing to Kafka, it can hold the join open well past the requested timeout. The loop should still attempt `terminate()` on all remaining processes even after the deadline expires.

findings.title: Docstring claims 'one process per shard' but default is one process total
findings.body: The class docstring says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1 (see src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py), so in the default configuration a single process handles all assigned shards. The docstring should describe the actual behavior (one process per shard-group, capped by max_processes).

findings.title: max_processes=0 silently means 'all shards' instead of being rejected
findings.body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses `or`, so a falsy value of 0 falls back to one process per shard. An operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` (a plausible typo or misconfiguration) will unexpectedly spawn one process per shard rather than getting an error. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(...)` and/or validate the CLI option is >= 1.

findings.title: Memory backpressure aggregation across per-process buffers may double-count Redis clusters
findings.body: `submit()` now aggregates `get_memory_info()` from each per-shard-group buffer. If `get_memory_info()` reports at the Redis cluster/connection level (rather than strictly per shard), clusters whose shards are split across multiple process groups will be counted multiple times in both `used` and `available`, weighting those clusters by how many buffers touch them and skewing the `used/available` ratio used to trigger hard backpressure (pausing the whole consumer). Verify that per-buffer aggregation yields the same totals as the previous single-buffer call for the same shard set; if not, deduplicate by cluster before summing.
